chapter_theme: The women are brought back across the wasteland and rejoined with the hero in tears and joy; the poet turns to the wedding of Ilakkanai, where an astrologer names the days, a hundred and eight elephants are readied, a herald-drum orders feasting and decking, and the city keeps the days in music, flowers and gifts.

cast.role: the hero, never named in this chapter's verses
the women, joined with the hero before, brought back across the wasteland
the astrologer who lays out the days
the king for whom the astrologer lays out the days, called elephant-lord
the drummer-heralds seated on the battle elephant
the people of the city who dress, decorate and give

2378.reading: The hero with the saffron-smeared mountain chest bids that the women who were joined with him be brought, and they are fetched through the lonely wasteland and handed over with grace.
2378.nuance: The verse names neither the hero nor the women; they are the ones he asked for in the preceding verses, which this chapter's first verse cannot show.
2378.event: At the hero's word the women are brought across the desert and given back to him.

2379.reading: The women, like peacocks, step down from the guarded jewelled palanquin, lightning-slender, as if they had seen release, in a place where bees and birds that never saw the sun or the moon tremble.
2379.nuance: The simile of those who have seen release (வீடு கண்டவர்) is for their relief and not a doctrinal statement.
2379.event: The women alight from the palanquin.

2380.reading: Withered in body, in the garlands and sandal of the day before, yet with no loss of gold ornament, they fall at their beloved's lotus feet while pearls of joy drop from their blue-lily eyes.
2380.event: The women fall at their lord's feet and weep with joy.

2381.reading: As he lifts and embraces them against his mountain-like chest, their long eyes, bearing tears and trembling, dart like a pair of carp in stirred water.
2381.event: The hero embraces the women, who weep and tremble.

2382.reading: Like forest jasmine buds scorched in the summer and then meeting the rain clouds, the proud women lose their pining and grief at the touch of their husband's honeyed chest, and shine.
2382.event: The women's grief ends in their husband's embrace.

2383.reading: The fish-eyed women set right their anklets and brow marks, wear fragrant garlands, paint the saffron creeper on their breasts and put on bamboo-bright shoulder pearls.

2384.reading: Their wide eyes, bright like fish that have fed on poison, roll and glance; as the jewelled girdles slip and spill, the slender-waisted ones shine, and he stayed with them.
2384.nuance: மாதோ at the end ends the scene; he who stayed is the hero, never named here.
2384.event: Civakan passes the time with the women.

2385.reading: The poet turns from these women to a new bride, Ilakkanai, whose gold-ringed small feet, narrow waist and bright jewelled girdle he describes, and says he will now tell her wedding rite.
2385.nuance: The line 'we shall tell' makes the poet speak in the first person plural, as the poets of the Cintamani do when opening a new tale.
2385.event: The poet announces the story of Ilakkanai's wedding.

2386.reading: A learned king, who finishes coming deeds in their due hour even apart from fate, owner of crowned elephants and a golden litter, has a great astrologer set out the days for the elephant-lord.
2386.nuance: Line 2 says he brings about a coming deed in its hour even apart from fate (ஊழின் அன்றியும்); the text does not say whether this places hour above karma.
2386.event: The astrologer lays out the auspicious days for the king.

claims.claim: an astrologer can bring a coming event to pass at its fixed hour even when fate does not decree it

2387.reading: On the great day the astrologer named for the king, a hundred and eight rutting elephants are made ready, wearing garlands and brow marks, white as silver hills.
2387.event: A hundred and eight elephants are dressed for the day.

2388.reading: They dress the proclaimers in white cloth and sandal, hang ear-rings and flowers and pearls on them and seat them on a battle elephant so that they can beat the wedding drum.
2388.event: Drummers are set on an elephant to proclaim the wedding.

2389.reading: The proclaimer cries: listen, wear pearl strings and sandal, bear the flower crest though the waist ache, put on fine cloth.
2389.event: The drum announces that all must dress in finery for the wedding.

2390.reading: Adorn the children and the whole body with jewels, he says; for seven days none may eat anything but the milk-nectar made by the generous lord's word, whatever the heart wants.
2390.nuance: The first half of line 1, and what பிட்டம் means, turn on a rare word; the sense of the command is clear.
2390.event: The drum commands feasting only on milk-nectar for seven days.

2391.reading: Plant plantain and fruit-laden areca, hang garlands, spread pots of aloe smoke, make lute-song and dance in every place, raise many golden flags like a cloven sky.
2391.event: The drum orders the city to be decked.

2392.reading: For the seven days of the king's wedding the ill-behaved rutting elephants are to be kept away, and the drum thundered out its order that the great city by the dark sea live.
2392.nuance: The king (மன்னவன்) whose wedding it is is not named; it is the king of the earlier verses, not necessarily the hero.
2392.event: The drum is beaten and the city is told to keep the wedding days.

2393.reading: After the drum six days passed, and everywhere white bangles swelled; lutes, flutes, drums and the thannumai sounded like thunder in the sky.

2394.reading: Women with parrot-sweet speech scattered flower dust like sky-lamps, sandal that lit the eyes, and flowers for the bali, brightening the earth.
2394.event: Women sprinkle flowers and sandal for the offering.

2395.reading: The steam of the milk boiling in pots rose in the mansions like thin silk shrouding them from the outside.

2396.reading: The red lac paint with which fair women, bowing, anointed the soles of the small feet spread over the ground like red sky at dusk.

2397.reading: The dressers' lamps, looking into the mirror, held the bees at dusk in the gaze of the garlands as moons held in a hand.
2397.nuance: The simile of line 1 is hard to follow; the verse's own subject is the mirrors in which dressers see themselves.

2398.reading: Golden gates rose through the clouds, garlands hung from the banners, and rows of pots lined the streets of the cloud-high city.

2399.reading: Dancers' anklets, songs, lutes and drums rang together so that the mansion city was like a great sea.

2400.reading: The dust of flowers and sandal and the smoke of incense seemed as if Indra's city had come to hold a festival here.

2401.reading: They poured sugar and ghee in rivers, gave milk-nectar to all who begged, and bade them take away fine cloth and jewels, even carrying them for them.
2401.event: The people feed and give to all who come.

2402.reading: They filled coconuts with jackfruit, plantain and mango fruit, pressed juices and sugarcane juice, and gave them to drink.
2402.event: The people give fruit drinks to all.

links.note: In 1062 the astrologers fix the day and the party sets out for a bride; here the astrologer lays out the days for the elephant-lord and the wedding is carried out on the day named.
links.teaches: The astrologer's fixing of the day is the Cintamani's regular first step in a royal marriage, and here it gains a royal scale: a hundred and eight dressed elephants and a seven-day city festival.

links.note: 1687 has the wedding announced with the drum and the whole world knowing; 2388 shows how it is done, with the proclaimers dressed in white and sandal and carried on a battle elephant.
links.teaches: The wedding drum is a royal herald's act with its own costume and mount, which the earlier wedding announcement only names.

links.note: Naladiyar says a wife married on a fixed day, with the drum beaten that many may know, is the wife a man should keep to; the epic shows that drum beaten from an elephant and the day set by an astrologer.
links.teaches: The Naladiyar's drum and fixed day are the public face of a marriage, which the epic acts out as a city-wide command.

gains.a: the epic's drum is given its moral weight, since a bond announced to all is the bond that shuts the husband off from another's wife
gains.b: the Naladiyar's drum and fixed day, only named in the quatrain, get a full royal scene: the herald, the elephant, the seven days of orders

links.note: The Akananuru man remembers a wedding of sand spread under a pandal, lamps and garlands at an auspicious dawn; the Cintamani's order has plantain and areca, aloe pots, lute and dance and golden flags across the city.
links.teaches: The same wedding adornments grow from a household's sand pandal to a king's command that the whole city be decked, and so show how rank changes the scale and not the parts.

gains.a: the epic's royal decking is seen to rest on the household's pandal, sand and lamps, which it enlarges and does not replace
gains.b: the Akananuru wedding, remembered only in the bride and groom's house, is set beside a city-wide wedding and shows how small and private it is

links.note: In 605 the drum proclaims alms to ascetics and hard penance while still in the body; in 2389 the drum cries to wear pearls and sandal and dress in fine cloth.
links.teaches: The one royal drum serves both a call to wear away the body in penance and a call to adorn it, so the epic's ideals of renunciation and of festival sit side by side without being reconciled.

links.note: The Naladiyar says the same wedding drums that sound in the hall may be funeral drums that very day; here a wedding drum thunders for seven days and the city is told to live.
links.teaches: The Cintamani's wedding drum is heard here only as joy, while the Naladiyar hears in the same sound the fragility of the groom's life, so the two give opposing readings of the same instrument.

gains.a: the epic's drum gets a shadow of impermanence which the Jain poet leaves unspoken here but may mean the reader to carry from the epic's end
gains.b: the Naladiyar's warning is given a concrete scene of seven days of festival to be undone, not only the bare image of a drum

new_concepts.gloss: the wedding; the rite that makes a marriage
new_concepts.label_source: the label is the house word declared in earlier chapters; these verses use மணவினை (2392) and கடிவினை (2385)

new_concepts.gloss: the festival; a public feast of a god or a town
new_concepts.label_source: label as declared in earlier Cintamani chapters; the verses show the city keeping the wedding days (2393-2402) and 2400 names a festival (சாறு)

new_concepts.gloss: music: the lute, melody, mode and the sounds compared to them
new_concepts.label_source: the verses name the lute (யாழ், 2391, 2393, 2399), drum (முழா, 2393) and song (பாடல், 2399)

source_issues: 2378-2384: the verses carry no name for the hero or the women; they continue from the last verses of the preceding chapter.
2390 line 1 பிள்ளை வெண்பிறைச் சிறுநுதற் பெரும்பிட்ட மணிமின் is hard to construe (பிட்டம்).
